tells.name: “delve” and kin
tells.what: The first famous tell. “Delve into”, “delves”, “delving”.
tells.fix: Say what you will do (“look at”, “compare”, “list”).

tells.name: “tapestry”, “testament to”, “realm”
tells.what: Ornate nouns used as filler metaphors.

detect.pattern: \b(?:rich |intricate |vibrant )?tapestry\b|\ba testament to\b|\brealm of\b|\btreasure trove\b|\bbeacon of\b|\bsymphony of\b

tells.fix: Name the things the metaphor stands in for.

examples.good: Greek, Turkish and Armenian families on one street

tells.name: “landscape”, “ever-evolving”, “in today’s world”
tells.what: Openers that place the topic in a vague, shifting world.
tells.fix: Start with the specific fact.

examples.bad: In today’s fast-paced digital landscape, teams need speed.

tells.name: “underscores”, “showcasing”, “pivotal”, “crucial”
tells.what: Academic-sounding verbs and adjectives of emphasis.
tells.fix: Cut the emphasis word and state the fact.

examples.bad: This underscores the pivotal role of caching.
examples.good: Caching cut p95 latency from 800ms to 90ms.

tells.name: “It’s important to note”, “It’s worth noting”
tells.what: Throat-clearing before a point.

detect.pattern: \bit(?:'|’)?s (?:important|worth|crucial|essential) (?:to note|noting|to remember|mentioning|to understand)\b|\bit is (?:important|worth|crucial|essential) (?:to note|noting|to remember|mentioning|to understand)\b

tells.fix: Delete the preamble. The point stands without it.

tells.name: “As an AI language model”
tells.what: Model names itself to hedge or refuse.

detect.pattern: \bas an ai(?: language model| assistant)?\b|\bmy (?:training data|knowledge cutoff)\b

tells.fix: Drop it. Answer, or say plainly what you can’t do.

tells.name: “streamline”, “unlock”, “elevate”, “leverage”, “foster”
tells.what: Pitch-deck verbs where nobody is pitching.
tells.fix: Use the plain verb (“use”, “speed up”, “let you”, “help”).

tells.name: “robust”, “holistic”, “nuanced”, “comprehensive”
tells.what: Abstract quality adjectives that sound careful and say little.
tells.fix: Name the property (“handles 10k req/s”, “covers all 50 states”).

tells.name: “journey”, “embark”, “navigate”, “bustling”, “nestled”
tells.what: Travel and scenery words used for things that are not trips or places.

tells.name: “genuinely”, “a genuine”, “is a genuinely”
tells.what: Sincerity markers. The current Claude tell, the way “delve” was GPT’s.
tells.fix: Delete it. If the claim needs it to be believed, add evidence instead.

examples.bad: This is a genuinely useful tool.
examples.good: This tool saved us a day per release.

tells.name: “That distinction matters”, “Why X matters”
tells.what: Announces that something is important instead of showing the stakes.
tells.fix: Show what goes wrong without it. Readers will see that it matters.

tells.name: “The practical takeaway”, “In practice”, “trade-off is”
tells.what: Signposts that label the next sentence as the useful part.

detect.pattern: \bthe (?:practical|key|real|main) takeaway\b|\bthe trade-?off is\b|\btaken together\b|\bjust as importantly\b|\bearns its (?:place|keep)\b

tells.fix: Drop the label and give the takeaway.

tells.name: “incredibly”, “absolutely”, “massive”, “profound”
tells.what: Adverbs and adjectives that add force but no information.
tells.fix: Delete the intensifier. If the sentence goes flat, it needs a number or example.

tells.name: “Furthermore”, “Additionally”, “Moreover”
tells.what: Essay connectors opening sentence after sentence.
tells.fix: Drop the connector, or use “and”, “also”, “so”.

tells.name: “the single most”, “the most consequential”
tells.what: Emphatic rankings nobody asked for.
tells.fix: Drop the ranking, or back it with the comparison.

tells.name: “a particular kind of”, “exactly the kind of”
tells.what: Gestures at a category without naming it.

detect.pattern: \b(?:a|this|that) particular kind of\b|\bexactly the kind of\b

tells.fix: Name the kind.

tells.name: “may provide”, “not necessarily”, “not automatically”
tells.what: Stacked hedges that leave no claim standing.
tells.fix: Commit, or say what the doubt is and why.

tells.name: “This comprehensive guide will walk you through”
tells.label: “This comprehensive guide”
tells.what: The article describes itself before saying anything.

detect.pattern: \bthis (?:comprehensive |practical |complete |ultimate )?(?:guide|article|post) (?:will )?(?:walks?|takes?|explores?|covers?|dives?)\b|\blet(?:'|’)?s (?:explore|dive in|take a closer look)\b|\blet us explore\b|\bin this (?:article|guide|post),? we(?:'|’)?(?:ll| will)\b|\bbefore diving into\b

tells.fix: Cut the paragraph. Start with the first real point.

tells.name: “Whether you’re a beginner or an expert”
tells.what: Addresses every possible reader at once.

detect.pattern: \bwhether you(?:'|’)?re\b|\bwhether you are\b|\byou(?:'|’)?ve likely\b|\byou have likely\b|\bif you(?:'|’)?re searching\b|\byou are searching\b

tells.fix: Write for one reader.

tells.name: “At its core”, “At the heart of”
tells.what: A promise of depth before a plain statement.

detect.pattern: \bat (?:its|their|the) (?:core|heart)\b|\bheart of (?:this|the matter)\b|\blies in its\b|\bvalue lies in\b

tells.fix: State the core thing.

tells.name: “It’s not X, it’s Y” / “not just X, but Y”
tells.what: Sets up a claim nobody made, then knocks it down.

detect.judge: Does the text deny a claim no one made in order to assert another?

tells.fix: State the real claim. Keep a contrast only when someone holds the other view.

examples.bad: This isn’t a tool, it’s a philosophy.
examples.good: The tool enforces one rule: every commit runs the tests.

tells.name: “less like X and more like Y”
tells.what: The softer cousin of contrastive negation. Rises when that one is suppressed.

graphite: less like a _ and more like

tells.fix: Describe Y on its own terms.

examples.bad: It feels less like a library and more like a language.
examples.good: It ships its own syntax and compiler.

tells.name: “rather than treating”, “not simply whether”
tells.what: Corrective framing. Defines a view by the wrong view it replaces. GPT’s form of contrastive negation.

detect.pattern: \brather than (?:treating|presenting|assuming|relying|focusing|merely|simply)\b|\binstead of (?:treating|assuming)\b|\bnot simply (?:whether|to|a|about)\b|\bwas not simply\b|\bthan relying (?:only|entirely|solely)\b|\bis a [\w-]+ rather than a\b

tells.fix: Say what to do. Skip the straw version.

tells.name: Rule of three
tells.what: Lists of three by reflex, often with rising rhythm.

detect.judge: Are three-item lists used where one or two items would carry the point?

tells.fix: Keep the strongest item. Use three only when there are three things.

tells.name: Em dash overuse
tells.what: Em dashes as the all-purpose joint. A real tell in 2025 that most newer models have dropped.
tells.fix: Use a period or comma. Keep a dash when you truly break off a thought.
tells.false_positives: People use plenty of em dashes too: 3.1 per 1,000 words in Graphite’s human articles. GPT-4.1 and GPT-5 ran at about 2.2 times that. GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 4 and 4.6, and both Gemini models now use far fewer than people; Claude Opus 5 sits near the human rate. Flag heavy density only.

tells.name: “Here’s the thing:”, “The kicker?”
tells.what: A staged pause before a punchline. Often fills in for banned em dashes.
tells.fix: Just say it.

tells.name: “X stops being Y and starts being Z”
tells.what: Turning-point drama for an ordinary change.
tells.fix: Describe the change and when it happens.

tells.name: One-line punchline paragraph
tells.what: A short, quotable last line that restates the point (“And that changes everything.”).

detect.judge: Does a section end on a short standalone sentence whose only job is to sound conclusive?

tells.fix: End on the last piece of information.

tells.name: “In conclusion”, summary recap
tells.what: A closing paragraph that repeats what was just said.

detect.pattern: ^(?:in conclusion|in summary|to sum up|to summarize|all in all|overall),|\bin conclusion\b

tells.fix: Cut the recap.

tells.name: Flat sentence rhythm
tells.what: Sentence after sentence of the same length. Reported as advice only; it does not separate model text from human text.
tells.fix: Mix lengths. Let a long sentence run when the thought needs it.
tells.false_positives: On 1,500 train topics, document-level variation (CV) had a human median of 0.51. GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra sit near 0.42, but Claude Opus 5 sits at 0.54, above people. Corporate human prose is often just as flat. Advisory only.

tells.name: No contractions
tells.what: “It is”, “do not”, “you are” everywhere. Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 and GPT-5.6 Sol nearly stopped contracting.
tells.fix: Contract where you would in speech.
tells.false_positives: Formal registers (legal, academic) that avoid contractions on purpose.

tells.name: “plays a pivotal role”, “marks a turning point”
tells.what: Claims that something matters a great deal, with no evidence.

detect.pattern: \bplays? an? (?:pivotal|crucial|key|vital|massive|significant|central) role\b|\bmarks? a (?:turning point|new era|pivotal moment)\b|\bcannot be overstated\b|\bstands as an?\b|\bserves as a (?:testament|reminder|beacon)\b

tells.fix: Show the effect. Readers will judge the size.

tells.name: “Experts say”, “Studies show”
tells.what: Appeals to unnamed authority.
tells.fix: Cite the source or drop the claim.

tells.name: “Great question!”, “You’re absolutely right!”
tells.what: Praise or agreement before the answer.
tells.fix: Start with the answer.

tells.name: “Let me know if you’d like me to...”
tells.what: A menu of follow-ups tacked onto every reply.

detect.pattern: \blet me know if you(?:'|’)?d like\b|\bwould you like me to\b|\bi hope this helps\b|\bfeel free to (?:ask|reach out|let me know)\b|\bhappy to help\b

tells.fix: Offer a next step only when there is an obvious one.

tells.name: Headers and bullets for a short answer
tells.what: Bold labels, nested bullets and section headers around a few sentences.
tells.fix: Write a paragraph when the content is a paragraph.

tells.name: Comments that restate the code
tells.what: “# Increment counter” over i += 1. “# Step 1:” scaffolding left in.

detect.judge: Does the comment say anything the next line doesn't?

tells.fix: Comment the why, or delete.

tells.name: Blanket try/except and silent fallbacks
tells.what: Broad exception handlers that log and carry on, or fallbacks that hide bugs.
tells.fix: Let it raise, or catch the specific error you can handle.

tells.name: Emoji in logs, CLI output and README headers
tells.what: Lines like “✅ Done!” or “🚀 Getting Started”.
tells.fix: Plain text. Use exit codes and log levels.

tells.name: Scaffolding for needs that don’t exist
tells.what: Factories, config flags, back-compat shims and interfaces with one caller.

detect.judge: Does this layer have more than one real caller or variant?

tells.fix: Inline it until a second case shows up.

tells.name: Purple-to-blue gradient, indigo accent
tells.what: Two-stop indigo or violet to blue or pink hero gradients. Tailwind indigo-500/600 as the brand color.
tells.fix: Derive the palette from the subject or brand.

tells.name: Cream and terracotta, or mono everything
tells.what: The “tasteful” fallback once purple is banned. Warm off-white, rust accent, serif headline, or all-monospace.
tells.fix: Same as purple. Derive from the subject.

tells.name: Inter for everything
tells.what: One sans at every size, no type contrast.
tells.fix: Pair a display face with a text face, or commit to one with real weight contrast.

tells.name: Centered hero with pill badge
tells.what: “✨ Now with AI” pill above a centered H1, subhead, two buttons.

detect.judge: Is the hero a centered pill, headline, subhead and two buttons?

tells.fix: Lead with the product itself (a screenshot, a demo, a real sentence).

tells.name: Three identical feature cards
tells.what: A row of three cards, icon on top, title, two lines of copy.

detect.judge: Is there a 3-column grid of same-shaped icon, title and blurb cards?

tells.fix: Show fewer features with more depth, or vary the layout per feature.

tells.name: Glass cards, glow blobs, sparkles
tells.what: Blurred cards over blurred color blobs. ✨ as the AI icon.
tells.fix: Flat surfaces. Spend contrast on content.

tells.name: Title Case Every Heading
tells.what: Headings in Title Case where sentence case fits.
tells.fix: Sentence case.
tells.false_positives: House styles that require title case.

tells.name: Middot-separated meta rows
tells.what: “5 min read · Design · 2026” strips under every title and card.
tells.fix: Show only the meta a reader uses.

tells.name: Gradient-filled headline text
tells.what: Headline words painted with a gradient via background-clip.
tells.fix: Solid text. Use weight or size for emphasis.

tells.name: Emoji as bullets and section icons
tells.what: Lists and headings led by 🚀, ✅, 💡, 🔥.
tells.fix: Drop them.

models.name: GPT-4.1
models.rules:
## Writing tells to avoid (tuned for GPT-4.1)

Readers spot these patterns as machine-made. Write the plain version instead.

- "This comprehensive guide will walk you through" → Cut the paragraph. Start with the first real point.
- "It's not X, it's Y" / "not just X, but Y" → State the real claim. Keep a contrast only when someone holds the other view. Instead of "This isn't a tool, it's a philosophy", write "The tool enforces one rule: every commit runs the tests".
- "plays a pivotal role", "marks a turning point" → Show the effect. Readers will judge the size.
- "rather than treating", "not simply whether" → Say what to do. Skip the straw version.
- "less like X and more like Y" → Describe Y on its own terms. Instead of "It feels less like a library and more like a language", write "It ships its own syntax and compiler".
- "underscores", "showcasing", "pivotal", "crucial" → Cut the emphasis word and state the fact. Instead of "This underscores the pivotal role of caching", write "Caching cut p95 latency from 800ms to 90ms".
- "At its core", "At the heart of" → State the core thing.
- "tapestry", "testament to", "realm" → Name the things the metaphor stands in for. Instead of "a rich tapestry of cultures", write "Greek, Turkish and Armenian families on one street".
- "It's important to note", "It's worth noting" → Delete the preamble. The point stands without it.
- "streamline", "unlock", "elevate", "leverage", "foster" → Use the plain verb ("use", "speed up", "let you", "help").

Phrases GPT-4.1 uses far more than people (Graphite, 2026): "approach ensures", "stands as", "article explores", "conclusion a", "this article explores", "stands as a", "approach not only", "approach ensures that", "let's explore how", "this approach not".

Prefer: specific nouns and numbers, contractions where speech would use them, one reader in mind, and endings that stop when the information does.

Check with `npx shibbo check <file>`.

- "rather than treating", "not simply whether" → Say what to do. Skip the straw version.
- "At its core", "At the heart of" → State the core thing.
- "tapestry", "testament to", "realm" → Name the things the metaphor stands in for. Instead of "a rich tapestry of cultures", write "Greek, Turkish and Armenian families on one street".
- "Furthermore", "Additionally", "Moreover" → Drop the connector, or use "and", "also", "so".

Phrases Gemini 2.5 Pro uses far more than people (Graphite, 2026): "approach ensures", "guide will walk", "into a powerful", "deep seated", "lies in its", "approach ensures that", "on a foundation", "a foundation of", "creates a powerful", "this commitment to".

Prefer: specific nouns and numbers, contractions where speech would use them, one reader in mind, and endings that stop when the information does.

Check with `npx shibbo check <file>`.

## Writing tells to avoid (tuned for Gemini 3.1 Pro)

Readers spot these patterns as machine-made. Write the plain version instead.

- "It's not X, it's Y" / "not just X, but Y" → State the real claim. Keep a contrast only when someone holds the other view. Instead of "This isn't a tool, it's a philosophy", write "The tool enforces one rule: every commit runs the tests".
- "This comprehensive guide will walk you through" → Cut the paragraph. Start with the first real point.
- "Whether you're a beginner or an expert" → Write for one reader.
- "plays a pivotal role", "marks a turning point" → Show the effect. Readers will judge the size.
- No contractions → Contract where you would in speech.
- "the single most", "the most consequential" → Drop the ranking, or back it with the comparison.
- "incredibly", "absolutely", "massive", "profound" → Delete the intensifier. If the sentence goes flat, it needs a number or example.
- "rather than treating", "not simply whether" → Say what to do. Skip the straw version.
- "less like X and more like Y" → Describe Y on its own terms. Instead of "It feels less like a library and more like a language", write "It ships its own syntax and compiler".
- "Furthermore", "Additionally", "Moreover" → Drop the connector, or use "and", "also", "so".

Phrases Gemini 3.1 Pro uses far more than people (Graphite, 2026): "this comprehensive guide", "you are searching", "let us explore", "helps to understand", "heart of this", "comprehensive guide will", "focus entirely on", "a massive role", "in this comprehensive", "whether you are".
